title: Generative Biology - Learning to Program Cellular Machines and Systems
speaker: Wendell Lim
content: Living cells are capable of sensing their environment, integrating this information, and making complex decisions. rawEventDetails: Speaker Wendell Lim Affiliation University of California San Francisco Details Event Description Living cells are capable of sensing their environment, integrating this information, and making complex decisions. These decisions are, at their heart, mediated by genetically encoded molecular circuits. In the field of synthetic biology, we have been engineering modular molecular components capable of sensing and actuating and using these components to create diverse cell-based biological programs. These include programming immune cells to search the body for combinatorial molecular signatures of disease (e.g., cancer, autoimmunity, and degeneration). We are also programming multicellular systems to understand the principles that drive multi-cellular self-organization, such as the development of tissues and organs. These synthetic biology tools and approaches are helping to define the fundamental logic underlying complex biological behaviors and provide new avenues to create useful synthetic cellular devices and living materials. Refreshments available 15 minutes before indicated time of seminar

rawEventDetails: Speaker Mattia Serra Affiliation University of California, San Diego Details Event Description Embryonic tissues undergo coordinated flows during avian gastrulation to establish the body plan. Here, we elucidate how tens of thousands of cells coordinate their behaviors to sculpt the chick embryo’s dynamic geometry (size and shape). Each of these two distinct geometric changes is associated with dynamic curves across which trajectories separate (kinematic repellers). Through physical modeling and experimental manipulations, we selectively eliminate either or both repellers in model and experiments, revealing their mechanistic origins. We find that embryo size is affected by the competition between extraembryonic epiboly and embryonic myosin-driven contraction—which persists even when mesoderm induction is blocked. Instead, the characteristic shape change from circular to pear-shaped arises from myosin-driven cell intercalations in the mesendoderm, irrespective of epiboly. These findings elucidate modular mechanisms that independently regulate embryo size and shape during development. Refreshments available 15 minutes before indicated time of seminar
